Problem: Bad supply transducer on pump skid, supply transducer was wired to 12v. 
Resolution: Arrived at store to assist technician. Checked in with MIC then checked the rack. Found the glycol
Return pressure around 10psi and the supply pressure around 38psi. Checked the E2 the return was reading None and the supply was reading 10psi. Found that the cables to the transducers were swapped. Corrected the cables and the return began reading but supply continued to read none. Checked the plug for the transducer and there was some corrosion. Replaced the cable with one that was on site. While replacing the cable noticed that the supply wire was connected to the 12vdc instead of 5. Corrected the supply voltage to the transducer with the new cable but it was still reading None. Changed the board and point which also did not work. Removed the transducer to inspect it, there was no debris inside the transducer or the angle valve. Replaced the transducer with the one that was previously in it and it’s working properly. Since the glycol pressure was low checked the freeze point of the hopper and it was -30° added water to get it to +5°. Checked the freeze point from the sales floor and it was +5°. Added glycol from the hopper to bring the return pressure to 25psi. There is a circuit setter in case 3-61c that is leaking. A technician will pick up a replacement valve on Monday to install.

Upon arrival, I checked in with the manager on site and investigated the reported warm case issue. Although the call was entered for the ice cream cases, I reviewed the E2 controller history and found no temperature alarms, abnormal temperature spikes, or issues with post-defrost recovery.

Further troubleshooting identified Cases 1 and 2 on Circuit 1C3 as running warm. After product was removed for access, I isolated and pumped down Case 2 to rack pressure, then removed and inspected the TXV inlet screen. The screen was found heavily restricted with debris and was cleaned and reinstalled. I repeated the same procedure on Case 1 and found its TXV inlet screen similarly restricted.

After restoring refrigeration, both cases showed improved operation; however, superheat remained elevated. Initial superheat on Case 1 was approximately 27°F. I adjusted both TXVs to increase refrigerant flow and monitored system performance. During testing, the circuit entered a scheduled defrost cycle. Once the circuit returned to refrigeration, I rechecked operating conditions and made minor final TXV adjustments.

Final superheat readings stabilized at approximately 11°F on Case 1 and 7°F on Case 2. Case temperatures were pulling down toward setpoint and maintaining temperature significantly better than prior to service. All operations were functioning normally at the time of departure. Call complete.
No injuries were reported on this job.

•	Any refrigeration appliance except for self-contains (e.g., bottle coolers on the store floor), regardless of charge size.
•	Any HVAC appliance, regardless of charge size
A note on HVAC units:
If refrigerant is required for an HVAC unit with multiple independent circuits/stages, keep in mind that each independent circuit is considered a separate appliance, so refrigerant adds on each circuit must be logged individually.
?	Example: if tech is working on PACU2, an HVAC unit with 4 separate circuits/stages, and wants to add gas to circuit 1 (PACU2a) and circuit 3 (PACU2c), tech or recordkeeper must enter a separate call log for PACU2a and PACU2c with the amount of refrigerant added.

Call logs are required to be entered in MyFacility within 72 hours of the refrigerant add. Failing to create a call log to record the refrigerant add within 72 hours is the equivalent of not getting approval to add the refrigerant. H-E-B will not pay for any refrigerant add that is not documented within the 72 hour window.

This requirement applies to ANY store/facility, any refrigerant type, including CO2, and any type of leak repair, including warranty work or any other special project.

It is wired to run all 8 compressor contactor control circuits which are beyond the amp rating of the one time delay - recommend either putting back to OEM spec , setting up the OEM individual time delays , and removing the bad time delay and wiring…..OR adding a relay capable of running all 8 contactors and replacing the field installed time delay.

Instead, technicians and/or vendor recordkeepers MUST create a “call log” in MyFacility within 72 hours of the refrigerant add, documenting: 
•	The appliance serviced.

•	Total amount of refrigerant recovered (if any)

•	Date refrigerant was added.

•	Any refrigeration appliance except for self-contains (e.g., bottle coolers on the store floor), regardless of charge size.
•	Any HVAC appliance, regardless of charge size
A note on HVAC units:
If refrigerant is required for an HVAC unit with multiple independent circuits/stages, keep in mind that each independent circuit is considered a separate appliance, so refrigerant adds on each circuit must be logged individually.
?	Example: if tech is working on PACU2, an HVAC unit with 4 separate circuits/stages, and wants to add gas to circuit 1 (PACU2a) and circuit 3 (PACU2c), tech or recordkeeper must enter a separate call log for PACU2a and PACU2c with the amount of refrigerant added.

Call logs are required to be entered in MyFacility within 72 hours of the refrigerant add. Failing to create a call log to record the refrigerant add within 72 hours is the equivalent of not getting approval to add the refrigerant. H-E-B will not pay for any refrigerant add that is not documented within the 72 hour window.

This requirement applies to ANY store/facility, any refrigerant type, including CO2, and any type of leak repair, including warranty work or any other special project.

Tech was NOT onsite for another call.

Upon arrival, I checked in using the third-party app and verified my arrival with the site manager. I then performed a walkthrough to locate the three-door reach-in freezer and the condenser unit that needed to be installed.

Once the equipment was located, I carefully lifted and positioned the condenser unit on top of the freezer. After securing the condenser to the top of the unit, I connected the suction and liquid lines.

With all piping connections completed, I performed a pressure test to verify there were no leaks in the system. While the pressure test was in progress, I completed the electrical inspection and troubleshooting. After discussing the findings with the Walmart technician, we determined that the following components should be replaced:

Accumulator
Suction service valve
Transducer
Discharge temperature sensor
Capacitor
Discharge pressure switch
Filter drier

I then contacted United Refrigeration to locate the required parts and placed the order. I also spoke with Brandon and received approval to proceed with the repairs.

Additionally, I found the drain pan heater to be in poor condition and recommended replacement.

I communicated with store management, who informed me that they would like the three-door freezer relocated to a different area of the store. They requested that the move be completed on Monday. I will relay this information to the office so the relocation can be scheduled accordingly.

Afterward, I pulled a deep vacuum on the system to remove all non-condensables and moisture. I then broke the vacuum with nitrogen and inspected the TXV screen and the liquid inlet screen at the compressor. Both screens were found to be clean and free of restrictions.

I pulled another vacuum on the system while awaiting the arrival of the replacement parts. Before leaving the site, I pressurized the system to 180 PSI with nitrogen.

Once the parts arrive will return to complete repairs
We need three techs out here Monday to move the reach in freezer

•Located the seafood dept. ice Flaker in the produce staging area, the unit on status light was off, and the bin was completely full, all the way above the level control sensors. Found that the EPR and suction ball valve were in a ball of ice, due to being un-insulated. Gauged up to the suction line, pressure was 1.7 psi, and the LLSV was still energized. With the motor not calling to be on, the LLSV should have de-energized also, and the condenser unit should not be running below 5-10 psi. 

•Checked the electrical panel, and found the L2 side of the solenoid wiring was bypassed at the relay. Corrected the wiring according to the schematic and the LLSV was now de-energized. Gained access to the roof, located the SISFO3 condensing unit for the ice flaker, the bottom of the suction accumulator was iced up, and found that the low pressure switch was set incorrectly to Cut-In @ 30 psi and Cut-Out @ 0 psi. Corrected the Cut-In to 20 psi and Cut-Out to 5 psi. 

•While the unit was still off, checked the scraper mechanics, and found that the scraper blade had a large piece of ice formed around it. De-iced the formation with hot water to allow better ice scraping, and less wear in the gears. Removed some of the ice into the transport bins below, to get the unit to turn on, unit turned on, checked power for the LLSV, and found that it has only been running on one leg of power, but the 7-8 replay terminals on the control module are not closing. Will need to replace the module. LLSV is only running on 120V, instead of 208V, but the unit is still able to produce ice. Could not source module locally, and it will need to be ordered.

Opened bottom panel and compared the evaporator probe reading to a pipe clamp measurement. Found the probe reading approximately 5 degrees colder than actual. Began preparations to pull a new sensor wire to the controller. Initiated a defrost and removed shelves to expose the back wall below the case controller. Began pulling the new sensor wire through the case using the old sensor wire, however the old wire disconnected during the process.

Removed additional shelving and back walls for access. Found the previous sensor wire had been spliced, causing the wire pull method to fail. Ran  wire and landed directly to the case controller. Due to the amount of shelving and back walls that had to be removed and reinstalled, this process took a significant amount of time to complete alone.

The new sensor wiring now has no splices for the most accurate readings. Also corrected return air mounting position. Confirmed the defrost sensor was mounted correctly.

Began checking for any additional causes of the previous ice buildup. Found one wire penetration that was not sealed and corrected it. Also found a panel behind the evaporator was not mounted properly. Carefully drilled a new mounting hole due to the tight working area and secured the panel correctly. Noted this was the same side of the evaporator where most of the ice buildup had occurred.

Part 2/2

While reassembling, found several tags behind the evaporator, some showing signs of being burned by the defrost heaters. Removed all tags. Adjusted the evaporator plenum and side seals to restore a proper airflow seal. Confirmed all defrost heaters were pulling proper amperage.

Reassembled all back walls, shelving, and bottom panels, and allowed the case to pull down to temperature.

Gained roof access to inspect the liquid line sight glass. Found the sight glass flashing. Checked temperature differential across the liquid line filter drier and found no measurable difference. Torched the receiver and found approximately 45% liquid level. Flashing sight glass condition should be further investigated.

Gauged up and verified operation of the remaining sensors, including the pressure transducer, discharge air sensor, and suction line sensor. Initially found the suction line sensor reading inaccurately. Repositioned and properly insulated the sensor, then verified the reading was accurate.

Contacted HEB EMS support to verify controller parameters. Left a message but did not receive a callback. Reviewed control settings and found them correct.

Determined the previous ice buildup was most likely caused by the combination of the failed evaporator sensor, stray tags behind the evaporator, airflow disruption from the improperly mounted panel and plenum seals, and the unsealed wire penetration. These issues have been corrected.

This call was for a water leak and ice accumulation within the POS freezer. We arrived on site, checked in with warehouse management, and were advised that the warehouse would be closing at 23:00. We then proceeded to size up the reported issue.
Inspection of the POS freezer revealed surface frost accumulation on the evaporator coils. Corrective action will include removal of the existing damaged drain piping, temporary removal of the drain line heater, installation of new drain piping, reinstallation of the drain line heater, and replacement of any required insulation.
At this time, the evaporator frost accumulation is expected to be resolved through a standard hot gas defrost cycle once proper drainage has been restored. No permanent repairs were completed during this visit due to the scope of work required and operational constraints.
Findings: Damaged/kinked condensate drain line caused by forklift impact and missing strip curtains contributing to frost accumulation.
Status: Incomplete – Follow-up overnight repair required to replace drain piping and restore proper condensate drainage.

I disabled this configuration and left the rack working with a suction set point of 43 psi and a deadband of 2 psi. After an hour of operation, the rack is at its set point, and all circuits, including the four 44-inch cases, are at their set point.

Problem:water leaking inside the unit

Resolution: Upon arrival, checked in with the store manager and proceeded to the bakery department to inspect the pizza self-contained unit. Upon inspection, found standing water inside the case. Removed panels and inspected the evaporator section. Found the evaporator drain pan full of water, causing water to overflow into the case.

Further investigation revealed the condensate drain line was restricted and not draining into the condensate pan. The condensate pan was dry, indicating the drain had likely been clogged for an extended period. Due to drain line location, removed the condenser fan assembly to gain access. Used a vacuum and drain adapter to clear sludge and debris from the drain line.

After clearing the restriction, poured water into the drain pan to verify proper drainage. Drain line operated normally and water flowed freely to the condensate pan. Monitored unit operation and confirmed no further water was entering the case. Reinstalled condenser fan assembly, secured all panels, and informed the bakery manager of findings and repairs. Unit operating normally at this time. No further issues found. Call complete.
